turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale's in the room. I got a fingerstick and vitals before I sat him down.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. Marcus, Dr. Ellison. You're here for the type 2 diabetes, yes?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. I'm just wiped out. Sugars won't come down and I'm sick of it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long have you felt this tired?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Couple weeks. Maybe more. Um, work's been garbage, doubles at the warehouse.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Chart has him on metformin one thousand milligrams twice a day and Lantus thirty units at bedtime.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Metformin, yeah, the thousand, morning and night, by mouth. The Lantus is not thirty. I draw up eighteen.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Eighteen units?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Eighteen. They dropped it after I went low. Well, actually, the nurse at the other clinic said cut it, and whoever typed thirty didn't talk to me.
[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): The med list from last month still says thirty units of insulin glargine nightly. I didn't change it.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): So we've got eighteen from you and thirty on the chart. I'm not guessing which is right today.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): It's eighteen. I'm the one sticking myself, not the computer.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you take that Lantus every night?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): The warehouse has me in at four a.m. half the week. If I shoot it and then I'm on the forklift I get shaky and sweaty, so I skip it.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many nights a week do you skip?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Work nights. Three, sometimes four. Days off I take the eighteen.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the metformin, you skip that too?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No. That one I take. Both doses. I'm not stupid about the pills.
[SEG0019] person_1 (NURSE): Fingerstick just now was two twelve milligrams per deciliter. He said his home fasting was one-eighty-something.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): I said one-eighty-something. The meter blurs when I'm half asleep. Don't put a fake number in there.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any lows besides those shaky mornings?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the main one. Shaky, sweaty, gotta sit down. Then I'm mad the rest of the shift.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vision changes? Spots, blurring, trouble reading?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Reading? I don't read at work. The lights in bay three are brutal, that's all. And my feet are what's annoying me.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm asking about your eyes, not the lights and not your feet. Any blurring or spots?
[SEG0026] person_1 (NURSE): He told me in the hall his vision's been blurry, especially driving in at four.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): I did not say that. Eyes are fine. I said the headlights glare. Don't put words in my mouth.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Feet then, since you brought them up. Numbness, tingling, pain?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Tingling. Right foot, mostly the toes. Not really pain.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): He said both feet, and that it's been about four months.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): I said the right. Left is fine. And it is not four months — three weeks, maybe a little over. She wasn't even listening.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Open sores, blisters, anything on the skin?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I look. Nothing open.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain or pressure on the job?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Can we not do a whole heart thing today? I'm tired.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Stomach's fine. I had a bad taco yesterday but that's not— never mind, I'm fine.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Surgeries?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Nope. Appendix is still in there, all of it.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family history of diabetes?
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): My dad. He was on insulin forever. Died at seventy-two, not from that, a stroke. Can we move on?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Never. Can't stand it.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): A beer Saturday if I'm off. That's it. Don't lecture me.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): Vitals when I brought him in: blood pressure one forty-six over eighty-four, heart rate eighty-two, oxygen ninety-seven percent, weight two hundred nine pounds.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Weight's whatever. The pressure thing, fine. I didn't argue with the cuff.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shoes off. I'm looking at the feet.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): They're cold. Floor's cold. Hurry up.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Skin's intact, no ulcers, no redness between the toes. Pulses are there. Monofilament is dull over the right great toe, left is okay.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Told you it was the right.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not changing the insulin dose today. Chart and what you draw don't match, and you're skipping it half the week.
[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): So I just keep doing eighteen when I don't skip? Great. Super helpful.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, stay at whatever you've actually been injecting until we see the bottle. Bring the Lantus pen and the pharmacy label next visit.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): It's a vial and syringes, not a pen. But fine, I'll bring it.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll do an A1c and a basic metabolic panel today, and a urine albumin.
[SEG0061] person_1 (NURSE): I can draw those before he leaves. The fingerstick's already done.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'm also referring you to ophthalmology for a dilated eye exam. I can't clear the retina from here.
[SEG0063] person_3 (PATIENT): Eyes are fine, I said. But whatever, I'll go if I have to.

[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): On work days, do not skip the Lantus just because you're afraid of a low. Keep glucose tablets in the truck and treat a low, then tell me. Check your feet every night, and if there's any break in the skin you call.
[SEG0065] person_3 (PATIENT): Glucose tablets. Feet. Yeah, I heard you.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): Last A1c you remember?
[SEG0067] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh. Somebody said eight-something. I don't have the paper.
[SEG0068] person_1 (NURSE): Last one in the chart, three months ago, was eight point four percent.
[SEG0069] person_3 (PATIENT): If you say so. I don't remember the date.

[SEG0070] person_2 (DOCTOR): That eight point four plus today's two twelve and the missed doses — my read is the diabetes isn't controlled, mostly from the skipped insulin. That's provisional until the new A1c.
[SEG0071] person_3 (PATIENT): So it's my fault. Fine.
[SEG0072] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's the missed doses, not a character thing. Come back in four weeks with the vial.
[SEG0073] person_3 (PATIENT): Four weeks. If they don't put me on doubles again.
[SEG0074] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four weeks either way. Nurse will book it and draw the labs.
[SEG0075] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book four weeks and send the eye referral out front. You want the labs now, Mr. Hale?
[SEG0076] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, get it over with. I want to go home and sleep.
[SEG0077] person_2 (DOCTOR): We're done in here. Labs, then you're out.
[SEG0078] person_3 (PATIENT): Finally.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Right-foot tingling is supported, but duration is patient-reported as about three weeks, not 3 weeks to 4 months.
bad.text: tingling in the right foot (category=neurological, status=present, duration=approximately 3 weeks to 4 months, temporality=current, body_site=right foot, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Insulin glargine/Lantus dose per patient is 18 units nightly; the recorded medication entry for Lantus is missing the dose.
Patient skips insulin glargine on work nights, about 3 to 4 nights per week, because taking it before early forklift shifts makes him feel shaky and sweaty.
Home fasting glucose was reported only approximately as 'one-eighty-something'; patient explicitly said not to record a fake exact number because he could not read the meter clearly.

Patient denied blurred vision or spots; he stated his eyes are fine and only reported headlight glare. The recorded symptom list includes blurry vision as present (disputed), but the patient’s denial of vision change is not captured as a negative finding.
Right foot tingling is mostly in the toes, not really painful.
Patient denied chest pain/pressure clearly was not established; when asked he gave an equivocal response: 'Sometimes, not really.'
Patient denied nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea individually; GI review is recorded generally but not the specific denied symptoms that were asked and answered.
Father died at age 72 from stroke, and patient stated it was not from diabetes.
No medication allergies: patient said 'No. Nothing.' in response to allergies to medicines.
Foot exam found no redness between the toes specifically; this is documented in physical exam but the patient also denied any open skin lesions after being asked about open sores/blisters.
Doctor is not changing the insulin dose today because the charted dose and the patient's actual injected dose do not match and the patient is skipping doses.
Doctor instructed patient to bring the insulin container to next visit, but the patient clarified he uses a vial and syringes, not a pen.

Last A1c in chart was 8.4% three months ago; the patient only recalled it as 'eight-something.' The prior completed A1c is incorrectly recorded as a completed procedure in this visit context rather than clearly historical.
